Selon le Phédon de Platon, Socrate boit: According to Plato's Phaedo, Socrates drinks the hemlock calmly and asks that a rooster be offered to Asclepius. This peaceful death was long doubted, since water hemlock causes convulsions. But the poison hemlock of the Athenians gradually paralyzes: Plato's account holds up.
Une coupe de ciguë ? Pour moi ? Socrate: A cup of hemlock? For me? Socrates drank it calmly. I'm spilling it on your pawn: three squares back. Remember Asclepius's rooster.
Criton, nous devons un coq à Asclépios ;: Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; pay the debt, and do not neglect it.
La phrase « Entia non sunt multiplicanda: The phrase “Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem” isn't found in Ockham. It was formulated by John Punch in 1639, three centuries later.
Le rasoir d'Ockham, qui n'a jamais écrit: Ockham's razor, who never wrote the famous phrase. The simplest hypothesis: I do nothing.
Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter nec: Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem.
En novembre 1619, en Allemagne, Descarte: In November 1619, in Germany, Descartes spends a day “shut up alone in a stove”, a heated room. There he conceives his method. He didn't sit inside the furnace.
Le poêle de Descartes. Je m'y enferme un: Descartes's stove. I shut myself in it for a day to meditate. Meanwhile, your pawn doubts, and moves back one square.
Je demeurais tout le jour enfermé seul d: I stayed the whole day shut up alone in a stove-heated room, where I had all the leisure to converse with my own thoughts.
Le sous-titre du Crépuscule des idoles e: The subtitle of Twilight of the Idols is “How to Philosophize with a Hammer”. A hammer that sounds out idols like a tuning fork, more than it smashes them.
Le marteau de Nietzsche. Je philosophe à: Nietzsche's hammer. I philosophize with a hammer on your board: one square has moved. The idols, I'm not sure.
How to philosophize with a hammer.
Diogène parcourait Athènes en plein jour: Diogenes walked through Athens in broad daylight with a lit lantern, saying: “I am looking for a man.”
La lanterne de Diogène. Je cherche un ho: Diogenes' lantern. I'm looking for a man, I find an enemy. I'm placing it on your path.
I am looking for a man.
